text: Instrument linear and binary search to count comparisons rather than time them. Fill in the three blanks.
choices: static int linear(int[] a, int x) { for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) { ___; if (a[i] == x) return i; } return -1; }
static int binary(int[] a, int x) {
while (lo <= hi) { ops++; int mid = ___;   // avoid overflow on huge arrays
if (a[mid] == x) return mid; else if (___) lo = mid + 1; else hi = mid - 1; }
int n = 1_000_000; int[] a = new int[n]; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) a[i] = i;
explanation: Verified: 1,000,000 against 20. The unsigned shift is worth noticing — `(lo + hi) / 2` overflows for arrays above about a billion, a bug that lived in the JDK's own binary search for nine years. Counting rather than timing is what lets you state what happens at a billion elements without running anything, which a measurement cannot.
